title: Fat Bear Week Returns: The Ultimate Chubby Championship
summary:
Get ready to vote for the chonkiest champion of the wild! Fat Bear Week, the annual contest to crown the fattest brown bear at Alaska's Katmai National Park, is back for its 12th year. From September 22 to 29, 2026, fans worldwide can vote online for their favorite fluffy giant.

Katmai National Park spans 4.1 million acres of volcanoes, rivers, and forests. It's home to about 2,200 brown bears that feast on salmon to build up fat reserves for the long winter. There are no roads into the park, but visitors can arrive by boat or plane to safely observe the bears.

The idea began in 2014 when Park Ranger Mike Fitz noticed two photos of the same bear—one from June and one from September. The bear had gained a massive amount of weight. Fitz and other rangers turned it into a one-day event called "Fat Bear Tuesday" on Facebook, where votes were counted through "likes." The next year, it expanded into a full week and drew hundreds of thousands of participants. By 2025, more than 1.7 million votes were cast from over 100 countries.

The competition is single-elimination: each day, fans vote in head-to-head matchups. The bear with the most votes advances until two remain. The final vote on September 29 decides the champion.

This year, 16 bears and bear families are competing. Bear 32, also known as Chunk, is back to defend his 2025 title after recovering from a broken jaw. He faces tough competition from Bear 164, or Bucky, who amazed fans by snatching leaping salmon out of the air. Bear 132 is raising three cubs—one got separated this summer and survived alone for several days before reuniting with its family. Bear 806 is caring for her own cub and an adopted young bear named Biggie.

Whether you root for the returning champion or a newcomer, Fat Bear Week is a fun way to celebrate these incredible animals and their wild Alaskan home.
why_it_matters: It shows how a small, playful idea from a few park rangers can become a global event — and how all that public attention can be turned into support for protecting wild animals and the places they live.

background_read: Katmai National Park (a huge protected area in Alaska known for its volcanoes and its many brown bears) sits along rivers where bears gather every summer to catch salmon leaping upstream. The park was protected in the early 1900s after a massive volcanic eruption reshaped the landscape.

Brown bears are omnivores that spend the warm months eating almost constantly. The fat they store then fuels them through hibernation — months of sleeping in a den through the cold Alaskan winter, when almost no food is available.

Fat Bear Week started as a one-day Facebook contest run by rangers from the National Park Service (the U.S. government agency that manages America's national parks). Rangers posted before-and-after photos of the same bears and asked the public to vote for the chubbiest, turning a biology lesson into an online game.

The contest works much like a sports bracket: fans compare photos and vote round by round until one bear wins. Because it is free and online, it has become one of the best-known wildlife events in the world and a big driver of traffic to the park's live bear cameras.

perspectives.description: The contest is free, funny and worldwide, and it gets millions of people thinking about hibernation, salmon runs and bear biology. Park supporters say the attention helps people care about protecting places like Katmai.

They worry that turning wild animals into a popularity contest can make people forget the serious threats bears face, such as shrinking salmon runs and habitat loss, and that 'cute' coverage can overshadow hard science.

They see Fat Bear Week as a textbook case of gamified science outreach, modelled on sports brackets, in which a small social-media idea by a few rangers scaled into a global event with almost no budget.

The next question is whether the popularity can be converted into money and long-term stewardship, for example through donations, live-camera programmes or similar brackets for other species and parks — without losing the educational core.
